title: Cascade - POC scoping: latency/throughput SLOs
next_steps: Sofia to send POC proposal + pricing sheet
Ethan to share benchmark matrix and test harness link (redwood-benchmarks.xlsx)
Cascade to provide 1-week sample traffic trace and baseline p95/p99 by 2026-03-09
action_items: Sofia Martinez: send POC proposal and pricing (due 2026-03-06)
Ethan Chu: prepare benchmark matrix, scripts, and runbook (due 2026-03-10)
Liam O'Connor: share sample traces and infra sizing docs (due 2026-03-09)
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez: All right hello everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sofia from Redwood Inference, AE on the account. We asked for this session to scope the POC around latency SLOs and throughput — specifically TTFT vs TPOT and how we'll measure p95/p99. 
[00:18] Maya Patel: Hi, Maya here. Thanks, yeah we're really focused on user-facing latency, we want to make sure our search assistant responds instantly.
[00:28] Liam O'Connor: Liam, infra. We'll be running this on dedicated hardware in our cloud account during the POC, likely N4-type GPUs, maybe we test on prem later.
[00:40] Ethan Chu: Ethan from Redwood SE — I'll drive the benchmark plan. Quick note, we'll need a sample traffic trace, and a few SLAs you care about.
[00:50] Priya Singh: Priya, PM. Success for us is 95th percentile under 200ms for first token on short prompts, and p99 under 500ms. But we want to validate that with our workload.
[01:05] Sofia Martinez: Great. Can you share current baselines? what you're seeing today with your stack?
[01:12] Maya Patel: Right now it's messy, we're on a mix of managed endpoints, p95 is around 450ms for small prompts and p99 spikes to 900ms occasionally during peaks. That's for hosted model calls to third-party APIs.
[01:26] Ethan Chu: Ok that gives us a starting point. For clarity: TTFT (time to first token) is usually the metric customers care about for interactivity; TPOT (we've seen it called tokens-per-output-time or time-per-output-token) is the per-token throughput once streaming starts. We should pick targets for both.
[01:45] Maya Patel: Yeah, correct. We want TTFT tight for chat and search. For generation-heavy flows, TPOT matters because it dictates streaming smoothness and cost.
[01:55] Liam O'Connor: One question — does Redwood measure TTFT at the edge or at the model container? We need to account for network hop inside VPC.
[02:04] Ethan Chu: Good call. In our measurement plan we define two measurements: 'service-level TTFT' which is measured from request entry at the Redwood frontend to first token emitted, and 'model-level TTFT' measured inside the inference worker to isolate network overhead. We'll provide both logs.
[02:23] Priya Singh: Sounds good. For targets, we're thinking p95 TTFT < 200ms, p99 < 450ms for prompts under 64 tokens. Does that sound realistic?
[02:33] Ethan Chu: On dedicated GPUs, with warm KV cache and optimized kernels, p95 150-200ms is achievable for small contexts with the right batching and quantization. p99 400-600ms is a practical tail target; if you need p99 < 300ms that's usually Dedicated + pinned capacity + strict batching config.
[02:52] Maya Patel: Ok. Also, we have an internal policy: any public-facing assistant must keep p99 < 500ms ideally.
[02:58] Sofia Martinez: Noted. Let's sketch the measurement plan: 1) replay your sample trace through the Redwood harness, 2) synthetic microbenchmarks to isolate TTFT vs TPOT (single-request latency), 3) full-load soak tests with realistic concurrency to measure tail under contention, 4) cache-cold vs cache-hot runs.
[03:20] Liam O'Connor: For synthetic tests, can you simulate hot KV cache and cold starts? We see big differences there.
[03:28] Ethan Chu: Absolutely — test matrix will include cold-starts (new worker, empty cache), warm-starts (hot KV hits at expected hit rates), and burst scenarios. We'll parameterize cache hit rate, batch size, concurrency.
[03:40] Maya Patel: What's the definition of TPOT again? Some folks use tokens/sec, others use ms/token.
[03:45] Ethan Chu: Good point — we'll standardize: TPOT we'll report as median ms/token and p95/p99 ms/token for streaming. Also report tokens/sec as aggregate throughput for the whole pool. So both representations.
[04:00] Priya Singh: For example targets: TPOT p95 <= 60ms/token and p99 <= 120ms/token on our target model for streaming short completions — is that reasonable?
[04:12] Ethan Chu: For 7B-ish models quantized and optimized, yes. For larger models or longer context windows those numbers will increase. We'll put model variants in the matrix.
[04:24] Sofia Martinez: We'll also capture cost per 1k tokens under each config so you can trade off latency vs cost.
[04:29] Maya Patel: Cost is important. If we need dedicated capacity to hit p99 targets it increases cost, we need the business case.
[04:36] Ethan Chu: Understood. We'll produce a cost/latency curve in the results.
[04:40] [00:04:40] Liam O'Connor: About measurement windows — do you compute p95/p99 over 1-minute, 5-minute, or 1-hour windows?
[04:48] Ethan Chu: We'll compute rolling p95/p99 over 5-minute windows and also report hourly aggregates. For SLA checks you can pick a window, many customers use 5-minute rolling tails for alerting and 1-hour aggregates for reporting.
[05:00] Maya Patel: Also want to make sure the test harness reproduces batching patterns — microbursts when user types, continuous streaming for long responses, and a mix.
[05:10] Ethan Chu: We'll replay your traces to preserve inter-arrival times; the harness supports configurable client-side concurrency and arrival patterns.
[05:18] Priya Singh: Timeline: how long for Redwood to set up the POC and run benchmarks?
[05:24] Sofia Martinez: Typical POC: 2 weeks to stand up and baseline, 1 week of run-in and tuning, 1 week of full benchmarks — total ~4 weeks. If you're ready, we can compress to 3 weeks with more parallel work.
[05:37] Liam O'Connor: We can provide sample traces within a week. If you can start benchmarks by 03/16 that works.
[05:43] Sofia Martinez: Great — we'll tentatively schedule on-prem/dedicated benchmark run the week of 2026-03-16.
[05:49] [00:05:49] Maya Patel: For success criteria, high-level: meet TTFT p95 and p99 targets for primary user flows, TPOT targets for streaming, and cost per 10k tokens below our threshold. Also an operational runbook for failover and fallback model variants.
[06:07] Ethan Chu: We'll include runbook items: canary deployment steps, automatic fallback to smaller model when latency spikes, circuit-breaker thresholds, and monitoring dashboards with histograms for tail latency.
[06:23] Priya Singh: Could you also include delta tests for quantized vs fp16? We suspect quantization will help cost but might affect quality.
[06:32] Ethan Chu: Yes. Matrix will include quantization profiles and a quality check (prompt set of critical queries) and we can run automatic evals to detect regressions.
[06:40] Maya Patel: Any compliance notes? We need SOC2 logs, audit trails.
[06:44] Sofia Martinez: Redwood provides audit logs, KMS integrations and private VPC options; we'll attach the security pack. We'll include notes about data retention for the POC.
[06:54] [00:06:54] Liam O'Connor: One more technical detail: how do you measure model-level TTFT? If we want to see pure model latency without network, what's the plan?
[07:02] Ethan Chu: We'll instrument the worker to log timestamps at request receive, model kernel start, first token emit. We'll provide both service-level and worker-level histograms. For privacy we can redact payloads.
[07:15] Maya Patel: Ok good. Also, define what constitutes 'warm' in terms of KV cache hit-rate — we typically see 60-70% prefix reuse for our app.
[07:25] Ethan Chu: We'll parameterize runs for 50%, 70%, and 90% hit rates. That'll show sensitivity.
[07:33] Sofia Martinez: For the POC acceptance criteria let's capture a concise list: (1) TTFT p95 <= 200ms and p99 <= 450ms on primary flow for prompts <64 tokens, (2) TPOT p95 <= 60ms/token and p99 <= 120ms/token for streaming on primary model, (3) Cost per 10k tokens under agreed threshold, (4) Runbook and dashboards delivered, (5) No regressions in quality on the evaluation prompt set.
[07:59] Maya Patel: That list looks right, but we might tweak numbers after the first baseline run.
[08:06] Ethan Chu: Absolutely. We'll call those initial targets and call out 'stretch' targets if you want more aggressive tails.
[08:12] Priya Singh: Regarding benchmarks, can we get the raw percentile logs so our infra team can ingest into our monitoring?
[08:18] Ethan Chu: Yes, we'll provide CSV/JSON exports of all latency histograms and per-request traces.
[08:24] [00:08:24] Liam O'Connor: Does Redwood's dedicated tier guarantee preemptible behavior or is it fully reserved? We care if nodes are reclaimed.
[08:33] Sofia Martinez: Dedicated provides reserved pools; we'll document the SLA. For strict p99 you should choose pinned capacity.
[08:40] Maya Patel: Is there an incremental cost to pin?
[08:43] Sofia Martinez: Yes, we'll include pricing options in the proposal.
[08:46] Maya Patel: Cool. Also, what about multi-region routing? We need EU and US presence.
[08:51] Ethan Chu: We can route by region and measure region-local TTFT. For the POC we'll focus on your primary region but can run parallel tests in EU if needed.
[08:59] [00:08:59] Priya Singh: Testing cadence — after the initial run who owns remediation/tuning?
[09:04] Sofia Martinez: Redwood SE will run tuning sessions with your infra team; we expect one joint tuning week. After that, we'll hand over the runbook and the results to your SREs.
[09:13] Maya Patel: Great. Any blockers from our side?
[09:15] Liam O'Connor: Just the sample traces and confirmation of target GPU types. We'll also need an account and VPC connectivity for the dedicated run.
[09:23] Sofia Martinez: We'll include a checklist in the follow-up with network steps.
[09:27] [00:09:27] Ethan Chu: I'll also attach the benchmark harness repo and an example script. Expect small transcription quirks in the logs — sometimes the agent timestamps drift but metric aggregates are solid.
[09:38] Maya Patel: Are there recommended models? We want open but high-quality — any Redwood suggestions?
[09:44] Ethan Chu: We'll propose two model families: a quantized 7B for low-cost low-latency use, and a 13B/70B for quality-sensitive flows. We'll include verified performance profiles in the matrix.
[09:56] Priya Singh: On quality checks, let's define a 30-prompt eval set that we care about and pass/fail thresholds.
[10:02] Ethan Chu: Works. We'll integrate that into the pipeline and report any perplexity/ROUGE-ish deltas and manual inspection notes.
[10:12] [00:10:12] Maya Patel: Anything else on TTFT measurement specifics?
[10:15] Ethan Chu: We'll provide histogram buckets geared to your targets (50ms,100ms,200ms,400ms,800ms). We'll also provide per-request traces for any outliers to debug root cause (batching, GC, kernel selection).
[10:27] Liam O'Connor: If we see p99 spikes, is the immediate mitigation to fall back to smaller models?
[10:32] Ethan Chu: Yes automated fallback to a compatible smaller model is part of the rollout plan. We also have circuit breakers and throttles.
[10:37] Sofia Martinez: Ok let's do a quick recap and record next steps.
[10:40] Maya Patel: Recap: Cascade to send traces by 03/09, Redwood to share proposal and benchmark matrix by 03/06, run benchmarks week of 03/16. Success criteria as discussed.
[10:54] Sofia Martinez: Perfect. Anything else?
[10:56] Priya Singh: No, that's it from me. Thanks.
[10:58] Sofia Martinez: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the proposal and the spreadsheet links.
[11:03] [00:11:03] -- End of recording --
